report.source_text: At the clinical ocular exam, the best corrected visual acuity was 0.1 in the right eye and 0.2 in left eye, while the intraocular noncontact pressure was 20 mmHg in both eyes. The slit lamp exam of the right eye revealed conjunctival injection, a peripheral, crescent-shaped corneal ulcer situated 2 mm from the limbus, extended on approximately 180° inferiorly and nasally (between 7:00 and 1:00 o’clock) (Fig. 1). The defect involving the epithelium and the superficial stroma is better illustrated after fluorescein staining (Fig. 2). Conjunctival blood vessels invading the peripheral margin of the ulcer were documented. The corneal sensitivity was normal.

clinician.trajectory_summary: The patient presented with chronic right eye pain, tearing, photophobia, and decreased vision for 4 months following ocular trauma. Initially treated for metaherpetic keratitis without improvement, the patient was found to have a progressive peripheral, crescent-shaped corneal ulcer. Extensive laboratory workup ruled out systemic autoimmune diseases (negative ANA, RF, ANCA, etc.) and general infectious causes (negative corneal cultures, negative hepatitis/syphilis screening). Despite initial treatment, the ulcer worsened with central migration. Following the exclusion of other etiologies, treatment with topical steroids was initiated, leading to significant improvement in visual acuity, complete regression of corneal blood vessels, and closure of the epithelial defect within one month.
